title: Calcium and autophagy connect photorespiratory oxidative signals with salicylic acid–mediated defense
content: In plants, photorespiration occurs in photosynthetically active tissues—such as mesophyll cells and guard cells—and is initiated in chloroplasts when Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) reacts with oxygen (O2), producing a 3-carbon 3-PGA (3-phosphoglycerate) and a 2-carbon 2-PG (2-phosphoglycolate). 2-PG is subsequently converted to glycolate and transported to peroxisomes, where glycolate-oxidase (GOX) oxidizes it to glyoxylate, producing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (Foyer et al 2009) (Fig. 1). H2O2, a relatively stable form of reactive oxygen species (ROS), acts as an intracellular signaling molecule but can cause oxidative damage when excessively produced (Waszczak et al 2018). Under normal conditions, H2O2 from photorespiration is efficiently removed by peroxisomal catalases, restricting oxidative stress (Foyer et al 2009) (Fig. 1).
